source_text: Pridie quam pugnaremus uideo in horomate hoc: uenisse Pomponium diaconum ad ostium carceris et pulsare uehementer. Et exiui ad eum et aperui ei; qui erat uestitus discinctam candidam, habens multiplices galliculas. Et dixit mihi: Perpetua, te expectamus, ueni. Et tenuit mihi manum, et coepimus ire per aspera loca et flexuosa. Uix tandem peruenimus anhelantes ad amphitheatrum, et induxit me in media arena, et dixit mihi: Noli pauere; hic sum tecum et conlaboro tecum. Et abiit. Et adspicio populum ingentem adtonitum. Et quia sciebam me ad bestias damnatam esse, mirabar quod non mitterentur mihi bestiae. Et exiuit quidam contra me Aegyptius foedus specie cum adiutoribus suis pugnaturus mecum. Ueniunt et ad me adolecentes decori adiutores et fautores mei. Et expoliata sum, et facta sum masculus. Et coeperunt me fautores mei oleo defricare, quomodo solent in agonem; et illum contra Aegyptium uideo in afa uolutantem. Et exiuit uir quidam mirae magnitudinis, ut etiam excederet fastigium amphitheatri, discinctatus purpuram inter duos clauos per medium pectus, habens et galliculas multiformes ex auro et argento factas, et ferens uirgam quasi lanista et ramum uiridem in quo erant mala aurea. Et petiit silentium et dixit: Hic Aegyptius si hanc uicerit, occidet illam gladio; haec si hunc uicerit, accipiet ramum istum. Et recessit. Et accessimus ad inuicem et coepimus mittere pugnos; ille mihi pedes adprehendere uolebat, ego autem illi calcibus faciem caedebam. Et sublata sum ab aere, et coepi eum sic caedere quasi terram non calcans. At ubi uidi moram fieri, iunxi manus, ut digitos in digitos mitterem, et adprehendi illi caput, et cecidit in faciem; et calcaui illi caput. Et coepit populus clamare et fautores mei psallere. Et accessi ad lanistam et accepi ramum. Et osculatus est me et dixit mihi: Filia, pax tecum. Et coepi ire cum gloria ad portam Sanauiuariam. Et experrecta sum. Et intellexi me non ad bestias, sed contra diabolum esse pugnaturam; sed sciebam mihi esse uictoriam. Hoc usque in pridie muneris egi; ipsius autem muneris actum si quis uoluerit scribat.
thought_title: Perpetua fights the Egyptian and wins the branch
orientation: Perpetua herself narrates in her prison diary the vision she saw the day before she is to fight in the public games.
pass_a_gloss: On the day before we were to fight I see in a nighttime vision this thing. Pomponius the deacon had come to the door of the prison and was knocking violently. And I went out to him and opened for him. He was dressed in a loose white robe, having many little sandals. And he said to me, Perpetua, we are waiting for you, come. And he held my hand, and we began to go through rough and winding places. Scarcely at last we arrived panting at the amphitheater, and he led me into the middle of the arena, and he said to me, Do not fear. I am here with you and I labor with you. And he went away. And I look at a huge amazed crowd. And because I knew that I had been condemned to wild beasts, I was wondering why wild beasts were not sent out against me. And there came out against me a certain Egyptian foul in appearance with his helpers to fight with me. There come also to me beautiful young men as my helpers and supporters. And I was stripped, and I was made male. And my supporters began to rub me down with oil, as they are accustomed to do for a contest. And I see that Egyptian opposite rolling in dust. And there came out a certain man of wonderful size, so that he even went beyond the top of the amphitheater, loosely clothed in purple between two stripes down the middle of the chest, having also richly wrought little sandals made from gold and silver, and carrying a staff like a trainer and a green branch on which there were golden apples. And he asked for silence and said, If this Egyptian defeats her, he will kill her with the sword. If she defeats him, she will receive this branch. And he withdrew. And we approached each other and began to hurl fists. He wanted to seize my feet, but I was striking his face with my heels. And I was lifted up by the air, and I began to strike him in this way as if not treading the ground. But when I saw a delay happening, I joined my hands so that I put fingers into fingers, and I seized his head, and he fell on his face. And I trampled his head. And the people began to shout and my supporters to sing. And I went up to the trainer and received the branch. And he kissed me and said to me, Daughter, peace be with you. And I began to go with glory to the Sanavivarian Gate. And I awoke. And I understood that I was going to fight not against wild beasts, but against the devil. But I knew that victory was mine. This much I did up to the day before the public games. Let whoever wishes write the account of the public games themselves.

lemmas.gloss: dust or sand of the arena as written

choices.why: marks this as the promised vision of outcome, not an ordinary dream
passive change of state before athletic combat, kept literal without explaining cause
keeps the arena preparation image as written while flagging uncertain spelling
proper arena gate name kept as a name rather than translated by function

pass_b_english: The day before we were to fight, I saw this in a nighttime vision. Pomponius the deacon came to the prison door and knocked hard. I went out to him and opened the door for him. He wore a loose white robe and many little sandals. He said to me, “Perpetua, we are waiting for you. Come.” He took my hand, and we started walking through rough, winding ground. We barely reached the amphitheater at last, out of breath, and he led me into the middle of the arena. He said to me, “Do not be afraid. I am here with you, and I am struggling alongside you.” Then he left.

I looked out at a huge crowd standing in shock. I knew I had been condemned to the wild beasts, so I was surprised that no wild beasts were sent out for me. Then an Egyptian came out against me to fight me, foul-looking, along with his helpers. Handsome young men also came to me as my helpers and supporters. I was stripped, and I was made male. My supporters began rubbing me down with oil, as fighters do before a contest, and I saw that Egyptian on the other side rolling in dust. Then a man of astonishing size came out, so tall that he rose even above the top of the amphitheater. He wore a loose purple robe with two stripes down the middle of his chest, and also ornate sandals made of gold and silver. He carried a staff like a trainer and a green branch hung with golden apples. He called for silence and said, “If this Egyptian defeats her, he will kill her with the sword. If she defeats him, she will receive this branch.” Then he stepped back.

We came together and started trading blows. He tried to grab my feet, but I kept striking his face with my heels. I was lifted into the air and began beating him as if I were not touching the ground. When I saw the fight dragging on, I clasped my hands to lace my fingers together, grabbed his head, and he fell flat on his face. I trampled his head. The crowd began to shout, and my supporters began to sing. I walked up to the trainer and took the branch. He kissed me and said to me, “Daughter, peace be with you.” I set off in glory toward the Sanavivarian Gate. Then I woke up. I understood that I would fight not against the wild beasts but against the devil, yet I knew the victory would be mine.
I have written this account up to the day before the public games. Let whoever wishes write the story of the public games themselves.
notes: horomate is kept as written for horamate; afa is kept as written and glossed as dust, spelling uncertain; galliculas is an unusual detail and is glossed literally as small sandals without adding an explanation.
